title: Commodification of nature

definition.text: A critical field of research on how natural things and processes are made tradable in markets, and what follows from that.

facts.text: Commodification turns goods and services that were not produced for sale into something that can be exchanged.
Drawing on Marx, Polanyi, O'Connor and Harvey, it is openly normative and critical, rooted in Marxist geography and political ecology.
It is used to challenge 'market environmentalism', which sees putting nature into markets as a fix for environmental damage.
At root, commodification makes qualitatively different things equivalent and exchangeable through money, and so commensurable.
Its origins lie in the rise of capitalism and the enclosure of the commons in England.
Emissions trading is a prominent example: it turns emissions into units bought and sold within an overall cap.
Climate justice movements explicitly oppose the commodification of nature and its resources.

contested_note: Market environmentalists see pricing nature as a solution to degradation, while critics argue commodification itself drives degradation and inequality.

title: Market environmentalism

definition.text: The view, prominent in environmental policy since the late 1980s, that environmental damage comes from nature lacking prices and that markets can fix it.

facts.text: It spread with neoliberalism, which gives priority to the free market and money-based relations.
This 'selling nature to save it' approach needs economic valuation, either indirectly through cost–benefit analysis and contingent valuation or by direct commodification.
Critics say it reduces species survival to a price that rises with rarity and extinction risk.
Critics see ecotourism and bioprospecting as forcing nature to earn its right to survive in the global market.
Selling nature to save it is also called green grabbing.
It assumes private actors act rationally on the best information, and that markets pool knowledge better than regulation.
It appeals to policymakers and private interests because it seeks solutions within the capitalist system.

contested_note: Its supporters treat markets as a conservation tool, while critics argue it subordinates nature to profit.

title: Critiques of commodifying nature

definition.text: The objections to turning nature into commodities, which fall into practical, moral and consequential problems.

facts.text: Practically, natural things resist: fish ecology shapes how fisheries can be privatized, and water's physical properties make it hard to commodify.
Morally, a single money value denies the many cultural and social values of nature; livelihoods, territorial rights and sacredness translate poorly into prices.
Markets handle fairness and equitable distribution poorly, and critics say commodification deepens inequality.
In consequence, efficiency and profit override other concerns, and market exchange is 'reason-blind' to ecological importance.
David Harvey argues there is something 'inherently anti-ecological' about capitalist commodification.

contested_note: These critiques are aimed against market environmentalism, whose proponents defend pricing nature.

title: Second contradiction of capitalism
article: Commodification of nature#Degradation of resources, underproduction of conditions

definition.text: James O'Connor's idea that capitalism degrades the environmental 'conditions of production' it depends on but cannot produce itself.

facts.text: Because nature's value cannot be fully counted in money, there is a tendency to overexploit and 'underproduce' it.
Capitalism is described as 'ecologically irrational', with a built-in tendency to overexploit its natural resource base.

definition.text: David Harvey's term for a new wave of enclosing the commons in which natural assets are released to capital at very low or no cost.

facts.text: Commodification 'stretches' across space and time and 'deepens' into more kinds of goods and services.
Bioprospecting and ecotourism are new 'commodity frontiers' alongside mining and agriculture.

title: Clive Spash

definition.text: An ecological economist known for critiques of mainstream environmental economics.

facts.text: He was among the first economists to work on biodiversity valuation, studying refusals to trade species for money as lexicographic preferences.
He found many contingent-valuation willingness-to-pay answers were charitable contributions, not trade prices.
He sees carbon trading as failing in theory and practice and favours rights-based approaches and regulation.

notes: Individual economist, not a founder of the field; per brief, people belong only in the People chapter. Concepts drawn out as Deliberative monetary valuation and Social ecological economics.

title: Deliberative monetary valuation
article: Clive Spash#Environmental Cost-Benefit Analysis, Contingent and Deliberative Valuation

definition.text: A set of approaches that combine individual willingness-to-pay valuation of environmental damage or protection with group discussion methods.

facts.text: It grew from evidence of fundamental failures in contingent valuation research used for public policy.
Social values are qualitatively different from the sum of individual values, a weakness of such studies.
A 'discourse based' alternative treats the valuation as a mutual agreement reached by contesting views.

definition.text: A proposed paradigm shift in ecological economics that integrates social, ecological and economic knowledge.

facts.text: It sees economies as emerging from and dependent on the structure and functioning of society and ecology.
It rejects reductionism and builds in value incommensurability and value pluralism.
Spash divides the field into social ecological economists, new environmental pragmatists and new resource economists.

definition.text: The branch of practical philosophy that sets out the kinds of argument that can be made for protecting nature and using natural resources sustainably.

facts.text: Its main competing views are anthropocentrism, ecocentrism (physiocentrism) and theocentrism.
It asks questions such as whether forests should be clear-cut for human consumption and which species should be valued for their own sake.
It influences environmental law, sociology, ecotheology, ecological economics, ecology and geography.
The field grew in response to Rachel Carson, Murray Bookchin and the first Earth Day in 1970.
Lynn White's 1967 paper on the roots of the ecological crisis and Garrett Hardin's 1968 'Tragedy of the Commons' had a crucial impact.
Alan Marshall sorts its approaches into libertarian extension, ecologic extension and conservation ethics.
Animal ethics and environmental ethics clash over duties to wild animals; some see them as incompatible, others as reconcilable.

definition.text: An approach to environmental ethics that stresses the interdependence and diversity of living things and gives intrinsic value to whole ecosystems.

facts.text: It is a scientific reflection on nature, where libertarian extension is a political one.
James Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis, treating Earth as one whole with its own ethical value, may belong here.

definition.text: Valuing the environment only for its usefulness to people, and protecting it as a means to human welfare.

facts.text: Because it rejects deep ecology's intrinsic value, it is often called 'shallow ecology'.
It may underlie government positions at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and the 1997 Kyoto summit.

definition.text: How the main theories of right action, consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics, are used to reason about the environment.

facts.text: Consequentialism judges actions by their results, such as whether they maximise well-being, which treats nature instrumentally.
Deontology says intrinsically valuable things must be protected as ends in themselves, so damaging nature is wrong in itself, not just a net loss.
Virtue ethics asks which character traits to cultivate, which avoids defining intrinsic value but is arguably anthropocentric.

title: Value of Earth

definition.text: The net worth of the planet, a disputed idea both in what 'value' means and in what counts as 'Earth'.

facts.text: It is usually equated with the total value of all ecosystem services.
A 1997 estimate put ecosystem services at $33 trillion a year, with a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion.
Against a combined world GNP of about $18 trillion, that implied ecosystems provide 1.8 times as much value as people create.
A later estimate gave $125 trillion a year for 2011, twice world GDP, with yearly losses of 4.3–20.2 trillion.

contested_note: Critics questioned the 1997 figures, especially the GNP comparison, though they accepted the basic approach.

conflicts.text: Combined world GNP closer to $28 trillion, making ecosystem services only 1.2 times as valuable.
conflicts.note: Disputes the $18 trillion GNP figure used in the 1997 comparison.

conflicts.text: World Bank total GDP in 1997 of $31 trillion, about equal to the ecosystem value.
conflicts.note: GDP rather than GNP; another benchmark for the same comparison.

title: Value pluralism

definition.text: The idea that there are several basic values that can all be right and yet conflict with one another.

facts.text: Conflicting values are often held to be incommensurable, with no objective ranking of their importance.
It opposes value monism, which says all values can be measured on or reduced to a single scale.
Unlike relativism, it accepts limits, such as when vital human needs are violated.
Isaiah Berlin first popularised a substantial account of it.
Alan Brown objects that values are commensurable because they can be compared by their contribution to human good.
Social ecological economics builds value incommensurability and value pluralism into its approach.

contested_note: Critics such as Alan Brown and Ronald Dworkin reject the claim that conflicting values cannot be compared.

title: Animal rights

definition.text: The philosophy that many or all sentient animals have moral worth apart from their usefulness to people, and that their basic interests, such as avoiding suffering, deserve the same consideration as similar human interests.

facts.text: In its narrow sense, animals have rights to life, liberty and freedom from torture that cannot be overridden by appeals to total welfare.
The argument from marginal cases says that if infants and cognitively disabled people have moral status, animals lacking no relevant trait must too.
The two main philosophical approaches are utilitarian, led by Peter Singer, and rights-based, led by Tom Regan and Gary Francione.
Regan argues animals are 'subjects-of-a-life' and so bearers of rights; Francione argues they need only the right not to be owned.
Unlike animal welfare advocates, who aim to reduce suffering, animal rights supporters often seek to abolish practices such as intensive farming, animal testing and hunting.
Critics such as Carl Cohen argue rights holders must be able to understand duties, which animals cannot.

contested_note: Philosophers such as Frey, Cohen, Posner and Scruton reject the claim that animals hold rights.

title: Commensurability

definition.text: Whether two values share a common measure; incommensurable values have no common standard or cannot be compared in a certain way.

facts.text: Two values such as freedom and security are incommensurable when no amount of one would make up for a loss of the other.
Two options are incomparable when neither is better and they are not exactly equally good.
Commodification makes different things commensurable by giving them a common exchange value in money.
Joseph Raz holds that genuine incomparability exists; Ruth Chang proposes a fourth relation, 'parity'; John Broome treats incomparability as vagueness.
Incomparability troubles consequentialism, since if outcomes cannot be compared neither action may be better.

contested_note: Philosophers disagree whether apparent incomparability is real, mere ignorance, parity or vagueness.

definition.text: An argument that two options are incomparable: if a tiny gain to one does not make it better than the other, they cannot have been exactly equal.

facts.text: In the example, adding 5 cents a year to a banking job should not tip the choice against a professor's job if the two are too different to compare.
The three ordinary comparisons, in Ruth Chang's terms, are better, worse and equally good.

definition.text: Karl Polanyi's term for things treated as market commodities though not made for sale: land, labour and money.

facts.text: It comes from Polanyi's 1944 book The Great Transformation.
Before markets ordered society, land, labour and money were embedded in social relations and governed by morals, religion and community.
Treating public goods and social necessities as commodities rather than protected rights may destabilise social systems.
Because nature originates outside capitalist production, its value cannot be fully counted in money, which tends towards overexploitation.
Resistance to treating the environment as a market good is seen as Polanyi's 'double movement' of forces for and against markets.

title: Land ethic

definition.text: A framework for how, ethically, people should regard the land.

facts.text: Aldo Leopold coined the term in A Sand County Almanac (1949), calling for an ethic covering humans' relation to land, animals and plants.
His basic principle: a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community.
It makes humans plain members and citizens of the land community rather than its conquerors.
Leopold saw two flaws in a land ethic based on economic self-interest: most members of an ecosystem have no economic worth, and conservation gets left to government.
Other land ethics rest on economics, utilitarianism, libertarianism, egalitarianism or ecology.
It is popular as a moderate view that balances human interests with a healthy, diverse natural environment.
Critics say it is vague and does not clearly explain why it should be adopted.

contested_note: Scholars debate what Leopold's land ethic asserts and whether it rests on human interests or the intrinsic value of nature.

definition.text: Land ethics that judge land use by the greatest good for people, or by individual property rights and freedom.

facts.text: Utilitarianism underpins industrial farming, which is defended for raising yields and lowering food prices.
Unlike a purely economic ethic, it can limit a farmer's profit if soil runoff damages neighbours' property.
Garrett Hardin argued in 1968 that the only solution to the tragedy of the commons was to give soil and water to private citizens.
Egalitarian land ethics arose in response, favouring equal access to land or food.

definition.text: Preferences in which a person prefers any amount of one good to any amount of another, looking at the second good only to break ties.

facts.text: The name comes from dictionary ordering, which attends to the first letter and only looks at the next letter in case of ties.
They are the classic example of rational preferences that cannot be represented by any utility function.
They are not continuous, which is why no real-valued utility function can capture them.
If everyone shares the same lexicographic preferences, ordinary general equilibrium cannot exist, because no one would sell.
Clive Spash used them to study ethically motivated refusals to trade species and ecosystems for money.
